title: October 2026 in Review
intro: A month of votes and verdicts: Alberta chose Canada, Quebec chose the Parti Québécois and B.C. chose the Conservatives. Hong Kong got its fire inquiry report, Beijing expelled top generals, and Americans head to the polls with prices rising.
notes: This is a Donna Daily special edition: original summaries and analysis drawn from the linked reporting. It does not replace the daily edition.

Left out for space or scope: the World Series and other sports, Stelco and steel-industry news, and several entertainment and tech stories. Some October stories are covered in the daily editions instead.

Opinion is split in two: “Our view” pieces are Donna Daily’s own analysis, written to present more than one side; “What columnists are arguing” paraphrases named writers at other outlets, with links to the originals.
provenance: Research pages were opened on Nov 2, 2026, between about 9:44 and 10:00 AM ET; individual check times were not logged, so none are shown on the story checks.
Globe and Mail stories were read through a subscriber session on Nov 2, 2026 at about 9:30 AM ET and are cited as “subscriber”; Donna Daily does not reproduce their text or photos.

Where a source could only be read through a search-index excerpt, the story check says so. Some sites (for example the New York Times, AP and the SCMP) refuse automated access; that is recorded as an access limit, not as a broken link.
Photos are from Wikimedia Commons under free licences or the public domain, checked on their file pages, cropped to 16:9 and credited under each picture.

stories.headline: Alberta votes three to one to stay in Canada, but backs tighter rules on newcomers
stories.deck: About 75% of voters rejected starting a legal process toward a binding separation referendum. The same ballot narrowly approved five immigration questions and rejected four constitutional ones.
stories.summary: Elections Alberta’s official count gave the “remain a province in Canada” option 74.95% (1,556,316 votes) against 25.05% for asking the government to begin the constitutional process for a binding separation vote. Turnout on that question was 70.4%, about 10 points above the 2023 provincial election. Questions on limiting immigration and restricting newcomers’ access to provincial programs passed with 52–58% support, while proposals to change how judges are chosen and to abolish the Senate failed. Premier Danielle Smith had urged a vote to remain while backing the other nine questions, according to the Globe.
stories.why: The result settles the separation question in Alberta for now, but the immigration votes give Premier Danielle Smith a mandate she can press against Ottawa.
stories.label: Official figures + reported
stories.note: The Globe’s early-results story ran on Oct 20; the official certified figures came from Elections Alberta on Oct 29.

stories.headline: Parti Québécois returns to power with a minority as the CAQ is wiped out
stories.deck: Paul St-Pierre Plamondon’s sovereigntists won about 60 of 127 seats on less than 30% of the vote, short of the 64 needed for a majority. The governing CAQ lost every seat, and Christine Fréchette quit as leader the next day.
stories.summary: The PQ grew from three seats in 2022 to roughly 60, while the Coalition Avenir Québec, which held 79 seats before the campaign, won none. The Liberals became the official opposition and the Conservatives won seats in the National Assembly for the first time in decades. St-Pierre Plamondon promised a third independence referendum but said it would wait until after Donald Trump leaves office, around 2029–30; as a minority premier he would need Québec Solidaire’s support to hold one.
stories.why: A sovereigntist government in Quebec reopens the national-unity file just as Ottawa is managing a trade war with the U.S., though a minority makes a referendum unlikely soon.
stories.label: Reported

stories.headline: B.C. Conservatives win a 64-seat majority; David Eby resigns after snap-election gamble
stories.deck: Lorne Doerkson’s Conservatives took 64 seats and about 48% of the vote, the party’s first majority in nearly a century. The NDP fell to 27 seats and Eby announced on election night that he would step down.
stories.summary: Eby called the early election saying his one-seat majority could not govern; polls flipped against him within days. Doerkson, a former rodeo rider and newspaper publisher who became interim leader only days before the writ, ran a more moderate campaign than his predecessor and promised to cut red tape, introduce no new taxes and sharply increase natural gas production. The Greens won two seats, including leader Emily Lowan’s.
stories.why: A right-of-centre majority in B.C. changes the balance among premiers on energy, Indigenous-rights legislation and dealings with Ottawa.
stories.label: Reported

stories.headline: Training-range fire at CFB Wainwright kills four soldiers and injures 39
stories.deck: A fire that began during live-fire training at the Alberta base spread rapidly when the wind changed, National Defence said. Nineteen of the injured were initially in critical condition.
stories.summary: The military says the fire started on an automatic grenade launcher range and was at first contained inside a designated danger area before accelerating. The chief of the defence staff told reporters the speed of the fire was the main factor in the deaths and injuries. The Canadian Forces Provost Marshal is investigating; no cause beyond the fire’s spread and the wind has been officially established.
stories.why: Four deaths in a single training exercise will put the military’s range-safety and fire-control procedures under close scrutiny.
stories.label: Official statement + reported

stories.headline: U.S. lifts 50% tariffs on nine Canadian product categories, but adds others
stories.deck: A White House order removed items such as plywood, plastic bags, corrugated boxes and refrigeration equipment from its 50% tariff list on Canadian goods. Some other products, including valves, carpets and shampoos, were added.
stories.summary: The change modifies the scope of the duties the administration imposed over what it calls Canadian discrimination against U.S. motor-vehicle trade. Removals take effect Oct 30. AP and the Globe linked the timing to close midterm races in border states such as Maine, where Republican Sen. Susan Collins faces a tough re-election. Canada’s broader trade dispute with Washington is unresolved.
stories.why: Relief for specific exporters is real, but the swap shows the tariff list can change quickly and politically, which makes planning hard for Canadian manufacturers.
stories.label: Official statement + reported

stories.dateLabel: Order Oct 30; hearing set for Nov 13
stories.headline: Judge orders federal officials to stop threatening election workers as DOJ presses ballot fights
stories.deck: A federal judge in California temporarily barred the Justice and Homeland Security departments from threatening or coercing state and local election officials. The administration is appealing.
stories.summary: Judge Trina Thompson’s temporary restraining order covers demands to set aside ballots, purge voters or stop processing them over alleged ineligibility, including threats of prosecution, and requires the Justice Department to report related subpoenas or search-warrant requests. It followed weeks in which the department sought to separate ballots from alleged noncitizens in California and Washington and asked Alaska to segregate ballots in its Senate race; an appeals court twice refused its California request. The order runs to Nov 16, with a hearing on a longer injunction on Nov 13.
stories.why: Elections in the U.S. are run by states. Whether federal agencies can pressure local officials during the count is a test of that system in the final days before the Nov 3 midterms.
stories.label: Reported + official statement
stories.note: The order’s terms are summarised from the court filing as described in a search excerpt and in news reports; the administration disputes that it intimidated anyone and has appealed.

stories.headline: Federal agents search Rep. Ilhan Omar’s Washington home in an immigration-records probe
stories.deck: Homeland Security Investigations agents executed a court-authorised warrant at the Minnesota Democrat’s home and seized phones, notebooks and her passport. Omar denies any wrongdoing.
stories.summary: Reports say the investigation concerns immigration paperwork from her family’s arrival in the U.S. when she was a child. The search came weeks before the midterms, which former Justice Department officials told NBC News broke a long-standing practice of avoiding overt steps against candidates close to an election. Omar later said she would have to move for safety reasons. The New York Times has reported that President Trump, a frequent critic of Omar, said in January that she should lose her citizenship.
stories.why: A criminal probe of a sitting member of Congress and prominent Trump critic, timed just before an election, has become a flashpoint over the use of federal law-enforcement power.
stories.label: Reported + allegation
stories.note: No charges had been reported as of publication; the warrant and supporting affidavit were not public.

stories.dateLabel: Theft Oct 29; FBI attribution about Nov 1
stories.headline: FBI blames North Korean hackers for record $6.3 billion theft from Binance
stories.deck: The FBI said the TraderTraitor group, which it also tied to last year’s Bybit hack, drained more than $6.3 billion from the world’s largest crypto exchange. Binance says customer funds are safe.
stories.summary: Investigators say the stolen assets were converted mainly into Ether and are likely being laundered through decentralised-finance and instant-swap services; the FBI asked exchanges to block transactions linked to listed addresses. Binance said it had replenished most of the stolen funds from its own reserves and would cover the rest. PBS reported the theft took about 20 minutes.
stories.why: It is the largest crypto theft on record and, if the attribution holds, a major new source of hard currency for North Korea’s weapons programmes.
stories.label: Official statement + reported
stories.note: Binance’s statements about replenishing funds are the company’s own claims.

stories.headline: Inflation climbs to 3.7% on fuel costs, and the Fed holds rates with two officials pushing for a hike
stories.deck: Consumer prices rose 3.7% in the year to September, driven by a 34% jump in gasoline. On Oct 28 the Federal Reserve kept its benchmark range at 3.75%–4%, with Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack dissenting in favour of an increase.
stories.summary: The Bureau of Labor Statistics said prices rose 0.6% in September alone; core inflation, which strips out food and energy, was a milder 2.6% over the year. Fuel oil was up 74% from a year earlier. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said the committee wanted more information before deciding its next move and announced fewer policy meetings in coming years.
stories.why: Prices at the pump were a top voter concern heading into the midterms, and a Fed split toward raising rates signals borrowing costs may not fall soon.
stories.label: Official figures + official statement

stories.headline: Wang Fuk Court inquiry blames a chain of failures; John Lee apologises and housing chief resigns
stories.deck: The independent committee’s report on last November’s Tai Po fire, which killed 168 people, found contractor misconduct, unsafe materials and lapses by regulators. Lee and senior officials bowed in apology, and Housing Secretary Winnie Ho stepped down.
stories.summary: Lee said Ho should bear political responsibility and announced a civil-service investigation and reforms across the departments involved in building safety and repairs. HKFP and other local media described a minister resigning over a disaster as rare in Hong Kong.
stories.why: It is the most significant act of political accountability in Hong Kong in years, and the reforms will shape how thousands of ageing estates are repaired.
stories.label: Official statement + reported

stories.headline: LegCo backs Hong Kong’s first five-year plan and the 2026 Policy Address after a three-day debate
stories.deck: Lawmakers passed non-binding motions on both blueprints after nearly 27 hours of debate. John Lee called the plan a strategic guide and the Policy Address its annual action plan.
stories.summary: The plan, aligned with mainland China’s 15th Five-Year Plan, centres on the Northern Metropolis, talent, commodity and gold trading, and “four centres and one hub” ambitions. RTHK reported that 88 lawmakers spoke. There was no organised opposition bloc in the chamber, which has been composed under rules requiring candidates to be vetted as patriots since 2021.
stories.why: The five-year plan is the first of its kind for Hong Kong and sets the government’s priorities through 2030.
stories.label: Official statement + reported

stories.headline: Hong Kong records its warmest October since 1884
stories.deck: The Observatory said the month’s mean temperature of 27.6°C was the highest for October on record, with record mean highs and lows too. It cited a very strong El Niño, a weak northeast monsoon and climate change.
stories.summary: The mean daily maximum was 30.5°C and the mean minimum 25.8°C, both October records. A stronger-than-usual high-pressure system over southern China also kept cooler air away.
stories.why: A hot autumn adds to cooling costs and heat stress for outdoor workers and for residents of poorly ventilated housing.
stories.label: Official figures

stories.headline: Most subdivided flats sign up for the grace period under Hong Kong’s new housing law
stories.deck: HKFP reported that about 70% of known subdivided units have registered under the Basic Housing Units regime. Registered flats get until 2030 to meet minimum standards; unregistered ones face enforcement from March 2027.
stories.summary: Owners have until Feb 28, 2027 to register existing units, which then enter a 36-month grace period to make alterations and seek recognition as “basic housing units” with minimum size, windows and their own toilet. Letting unregistered or unrecognised units becomes an offence from March 1, 2027. Government figures on applications were given in a reply to a lawmaker’s question on Oct 28.
stories.why: Tens of thousands of low-income households live in subdivided flats; how landlords respond will decide whether they get safer homes or face rent rises and displacement.
stories.label: Official figures + reported

stories.headline: Communist Party plenum confirms record expulsions, including former top general Zhang Youxia
stories.deck: The Central Committee’s fifth plenum adopted a resolution on strict party self-governance and ratified the expulsion of 33 senior officials, the most at a plenum since the Mao era. One was, until this year, the army’s top uniformed officer.
stories.summary: State media’s communiqué said the meeting fully affirmed the Politburo’s work and urged discipline ahead of a new round of party elections. Those expelled include former Politburo members Ma Xingrui and Zhang Youxia and former diplomat Liu Jianchao. Analysts quoted by the BBC, NPR and AP read the purge as Xi Jinping consolidating control before the 2027 party congress, where he is expected to seek a fourth term; several analysts note the Central Military Commission has been left with very few members.
stories.why: Fifth plenums usually set the stage for leadership changes; this one signals loyalty and discipline will decide who rises in 2027.
stories.label: State media + reported + analysis

stories.headline: Exports surge 36% and lift China’s growth to 4.5%, while shoppers stay cautious
stories.deck: September exports jumped 36.3% from a year earlier, led by AI-related hardware, producing a record monthly trade surplus of about $133.5 billion. Third-quarter GDP grew 4.5%, beating forecasts.
stories.summary: The nine-month surplus reached about $938 billion, putting a $1 trillion year in sight. Shipments to Southeast Asia rose even faster. At home, retail sales and property investment stayed weak, a split that economists say leaves growth leaning on foreign demand and invites more trade friction with the U.S., the EU and Asian neighbours.
stories.why: China’s export boom keeps its economy near target, but it is also the main driver of tariff disputes, including those that affect Canada and Hong Kong’s port trade.
stories.label: Official figures + reported

stories.headline: Magnitude-7.0 earthquake in Tibet’s Nagqu region kills 16
stories.deck: The quake struck Baqen County on the high plateau. State media later reported 76 injured and 339 homes damaged or destroyed, with no further deaths.
stories.summary: Rescuers worked in thin air and cold temperatures; officials then turned to assessing landslide and other geological risks from aftershocks. Independent reporting from the region is restricted, so most details come from Chinese official sources.
stories.why: It was China’s deadliest earthquake of the year, in a remote area where access for independent journalists is limited.
stories.label: Reported + state media

stories.headline: Kim Jong Un crosses into China as the long-delayed Yalu River bridge finally opens
stories.deck: The New Yalu River Bridge linking Dandong and Sinuiju opened to traffic on Oct 15 after more than a decade of delays. Kim made a one-day visit to Dandong on Oct 24 and met senior leader Wang Huning.
stories.summary: The four-lane bridge, about 3 km long, is meant to expand trade between the two neighbours. China’s foreign ministry said Kim also visited a Korean War memorial and a car factory and pledged closer co-operation.
stories.why: It is a visible sign of Beijing deepening ties with Pyongyang while Washington and Seoul press for sanctions to be enforced.

stories.headline: Social Security checks will rise 3.6% in 2027
stories.deck: About 76 million Social Security and SSI recipients get the cost-of-living increase. For retirees that is an average of roughly $75 a month, starting with January payments.
stories.summary: The adjustment follows the government’s inflation index for wage earners, which rose this year in part because of higher fuel prices. Increases for Supplemental Security Income begin with the payment at the end of December.
stories.why: For many older Americans the annual adjustment decides whether rising prices for gas and groceries can be absorbed.
stories.label: Official statement

stories.headline: The first new sunscreen ingredient in decades reaches U.S. store shelves
stories.deck: Sunscreens made with bemotrizinol (BEMT), long sold in Europe and Asia, began appearing in American stores after the FDA cleared the ingredient this year. Dermatologists say it offers broad UVA and UVB protection and goes on clear.
stories.summary: The U.S. had not added a new sunscreen active ingredient in about two decades, partly because sunscreens are regulated as over-the-counter drugs. Reports describe BEMT as long used abroad and well studied.
stories.why: Americans have had fewer sunscreen options than shoppers abroad; more choice may make daily sun protection easier, which matters for skin-cancer prevention.
stories.label: Reported + official statement

stories.headline: Ottawa moves to permanently bar assisted dying for mental illness alone and allow advance requests
stories.deck: The federal MAID Safeguards Act, Bill C-41, would cancel the expansion of medical assistance in dying to people whose only condition is a mental illness, due in March 2027. It would also let adults diagnosed with conditions such as Alzheimer’s request MAID in advance.
stories.summary: Justice Minister Sean Fraser said serious concerns remain about assessing mental-illness cases safely and consistently, echoing a joint parliamentary committee’s June recommendation. Advance requests would come with new safeguards, and a person would still need to be suffering intolerably when MAID is provided. Provinces would decide whether to offer advance requests. The bill must pass before March 17, 2027 to stop the scheduled expansion.
stories.why: The bill settles a decade-long debate over mental illness and MAID while opening a new path for people facing dementia, one of the most requested changes to the law.
stories.label: Official proposal + reported
stories.note: The Globe’s story on Ottawa’s plan is dated Oct 7 in our research notes; the bill itself was introduced Oct 27.

stories.dateLabel: Book out Oct 13; Globe interview Oct 17
stories.headline: Clara Hughes writes frankly about menopause, injury and depression in a new memoir
stories.deck: The six-time Olympic medallist’s Learning to Breathe follows the years after a 2021 knee injury, as hot flashes, mood swings and depression upended an athlete used to controlling her body.
stories.summary: Hughes, a long-time mental-health advocate who won Olympic medals in both cycling and speed skating, writes about losing the training routine that had steadied her, and about the help she sought, according to her publisher’s description and the Globe’s Life section.

stories.author: Donna Daily
stories.headline: Three votes, three messages: Canada’s month of sovereignty politics
stories.deck: In one month Alberta rejected a path to separation, Quebec elected a sovereigntist party, and B.C. swung hard to the right. Read together, they say less about breaking up Canada than about voters punishing incumbents and testing Ottawa.
stories.summary: Alberta’s 75% vote to remain is the clearest result, but the same ballot backed tougher limits on newcomers, a sign of anger that federal politics has not absorbed. In Quebec, the Parti Québécois won on frustration with a tired CAQ government, with less than 30% of the vote and a promise to delay any referendum; a minority leaves it dependent on other parties. In B.C., the Conservatives won by promising lower taxes and more natural gas, not by campaigning on the constitution. The case for worry is real: Premier Danielle Smith now has a mandate to push Ottawa on immigration, and the PQ will look for fights it can use. The case for calm is also real: no province voted to leave, and each government will be judged first on cost of living and services.
stories.why: For readers outside Canada: the unity question is back on the agenda, but the month’s results point to tougher bargaining with Ottawa rather than an imminent breakup.
stories.label: Our view

stories.author: Donna Daily
stories.headline: On the eve of the midterms, courts are acting as the referee for America’s election rules
stories.deck: A federal judge’s order on Oct 30 and the search of a congresswoman’s home weeks before voting show how much pressure now sits on the people and institutions that run and police elections.
stories.summary: Elections in the U.S. are run by states and counties, and the courts exist to settle disputes about the rules. That system worked as designed when a federal judge temporarily barred the Justice and Homeland Security departments from threatening or coercing state and local election officials, and set a hearing for Nov 13; the administration says it intimidated no one and is appealing. But each emergency order is a sign of strain, and supporters of the administration argue federal officials have a legitimate duty to police fraud. On the Omar case, the questions are about timing and process: federal investigators obtained a warrant, while former Justice Department officials say acting so close to an election breaks with long practice. Both concerns can be true. Voters are best served when election officials are left to do their jobs, investigations follow normal rules, and courts decide disputes quickly and in public.
stories.why: Confidence in the result of the midterms depends on all sides accepting that the referee’s calls are fair, whichever way they go.
stories.label: Our view

stories.author: Donna Daily
stories.headline: Accountability, two ways: Hong Kong’s bow and Beijing’s purge
stories.deck: In the same week, Hong Kong’s top officials bowed in apology after the Tai Po fire report and a minister resigned, while the Communist Party expelled 33 officials, including the military’s top-ranking general, Zhang Youxia, at a closed-door plenum.
stories.summary: Both are presented as accountability, but they work differently. Hong Kong’s came after a public inquiry with witnesses and hearings, and its findings can be read and argued over; critics say it should have gone further, and supporters say the government took responsibility in a way that is rare for the city. Beijing’s came through party discipline: the reasons given are brief, the evidence is not public, and outside analysts debate whether it is about corruption, loyalty or both. Neither system lets voters remove those in charge. But a public record, as in Hong Kong’s case, gives residents something to hold the government to when it promises reform.
stories.why: How each government handles failure shapes public trust, and the difference between open hearings and closed-door discipline is worth watching as both promise reform.
stories.label: Our view
